Sweep results · TSLA + MSFT · 2022-05-02 → 2022-11-18

Ontology evolution under a downstream gate: 72 runs across two tickers

A balanced 72-configuration experiment, run as two independent 36-run halves — TSLA labelled against a mixed news corpus, MSFT against a corpus filtered to MSFT alone. The evolved graph beat a text-only baseline in 28 of 36 runs in each half, while no hyperparameter, path-feature or corpus difference shifted the mean by more than the ordinary scatter between runs.

A · The system, and what was varied

What a run does. From a base ontology, an LLM proposes candidate extensions over several steps. Each candidate is one node type together with one relationship — say EarningsReport attached by HAS_EARNINGS_REPORT. Two are proposed per step; the graph is rebuilt under each, day-level features extracted, and an XGBoost classifier predicts next-day price direction. The step's winner is the higher validation AUC, and a gate accepts it only if it improves on the run's best so far. A run's result is the AUC of its final accepted ontology.

What it is compared against. Each run also scores a text-only baseline: mean-pooled article embeddings, no graph.

The design. Four hyperparameters vary at once. The full grid is 4 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 108 runs per ticker; we ran 36, chosen so every pair of settings occurs together equally often. Comparing steps=3 against steps=7, the two groups of 12 contain the same mix of every other factor, so a gap belongs to steps alone. (A strength-2 orthogonal array, OA(36, 4¹3³, 2), verified per half against both the config files and the returned MLflow runs: no missing combination, each pair occurring 3 or 4 times.)

Fixed across all 72 runs: 4 articles/day, 2 candidates per step, feature_mode=hybrid, single-addition gate with auc_drop_tolerance=0, 98 training days. Infrastructure: 8 × g5.xlarge vLLM workers, 6 embedding replicas, ephemeral Neo4j per job, on EKS.

The article set

TSLA draws its 4 articles/day from every ticker in the file; MSFT applies --filter-ticker, selecting MSFT articles before the per-day cap. Each labels the next-day direction of its own ticker.

How consistent is the lift?

The lift is a within-run contrast: each run's graph AUC against its own text baseline on the same validation days. It is positive in 28 of 36 runs in each half — the same count on both sides, from different labels and different corpora. Mean lift is +0.054 on one side and +0.044 on the other, a difference of 0.0095.

Set against that, the spread between runs is large: AUC varies by SD 0.065 (TSLA) and 0.064 (MSFT) across the 36 runs of a half — bigger than any factor effect in section D.

D · Hyperparameter effects

Runs vary far more than factors do. TSLA AUC has SD 0.065 around a grand mean of 0.617; MSFT SD 0.064 around 0.609. The furthest any factor level sits from its own grand mean is 0.028 (TSLA, hops = 4) and 0.036 (MSFT, hops = 3) — each well under half the ordinary scatter between runs.

E · Which ontology additions help?

720 addition records, 360 per ticker — one per (step, candidate). TSLA produced 32 node types across 80 distinct pairs, MSFT 37 across 90, plus one candidate that proposed a node type with no relationshisop at all (RegulatoryBody, step 5, rejected). The pair framing assumes that cannot happen; it happened once in 720.

How to measure it and why the obvious score does not work

Scoring an addition as "AUC minus the run's best so far" fails, because the gate makes that reference the running maximum. A candidate is then judged partly on how lucky its own run's first step happened to be. Candidate quality stays flat across steps while the reference climbs, so the share scored negative grows for that reason alone.

The unbiased comparison is between the two candidates within a step: same graph, same days, same point in the run, differing only in the type added. And at 42 validation days the size of a gap is not worth reading — only which one won. So each addition is scored by win rate: how often it beat the alternative proposed alongside it.

The ranking does not replicate.

The two together show the ordering is noise — the clearest argument in this report for why the second half was worth running.

Gate behaviourTSLAMSFT
additions accepted66 / 360 (18.3%)90 / 360 (25.0%)
mean Δ of accepted+0.029+0.018
mean Δ of rejected−0.119−0.107

The gate does discriminate in the right direction on both sides. On cost: steps=7 takes roughly 1.4× the compute of steps=3 and buys +0.016 AUC on TSLA and +0.029 on MSFT — both under a third of the run-to-run scatter — while accepting candidates at a fraction of the first-step rate.

What is not measured. An addition's absolute effect would be AUC(base + addition) − AUC(base), but the base graph is never scored: step 0 evaluates only the text baseline. Nothing here can say whether adding a type helps at all — only which types beat the alternatives they were proposed against.

F · Which differences survive a test

Which of the differences above hold up under a formal test. The run is the unit of analysis — 36 per half — so nothing rests on the precision of a single AUC: the ANOVA and Welch tests take their error term from the observed run-to-run scatter, the sign test from win counts alone.

G · Caveats

  • The halves differ in two ways at once — ticker and article filtering — so "filtering changed nothing" is a statement about the two halves as run, not a clean one-factor experiment.
  • 42 validation days against 488 dimensions. Individual AUCs are correspondingly imprecise, and run-to-run scatter exceeds every effect reported above.
  • The per-day article selection is tie-broken arbitrarily (section A).
  • n = 9–12 per factor level — adequate for large effects only. No effect size here should be read as precise.
  • Two tickers, one window, one market regime (May–November 2022).

H · Discussion and next steps

  • What the two halves jointly establish is a replicated set of negatives: path features do nothing, no hyperparameter separates from run-to-run scatter, the addition ranking does not survive a change of ticker, and the model memorises its training set completely. A methodological finding follows — a downstream-accuracy acceptance gate is unusable when run-to-run variability exceeds the effect size, and degrades into regression-to-the-maximum selection. That applies to the whole class of "LLM proposes schema, downstream metric accepts" designs, and contrasts with arun2025finreflectkg, which iterates inside a fixed schema and never faces it.
  • The corpus explanation is closed — tested directly, at full design strength, and it changed nothing. Worth stating positively: it removes an alternative explanation rather than leaving it open.
  • Log the day-level feature matrix. Nothing currently persists X and y, so every modelling question has cost a full sweep. Persisting them turns the next question into a notebook.
  • Cut 488 features to ~20 and fold the evaluation. Both are free and both attack the 1.0000 train AUC directly. These should come before any further spend.
  • Then buy sample size. Pooling cross-sectionally across tickers is the only route to resolving effects this small: 20 tickers × 42 validation days is roughly a twentyfold increase in observations.
  • !!Is next-day direction the right target? It is near a coin flip and may lack the signal to separate KG variants at any feasible sample size. Volatility direction, abnormal volume or |return| magnitude are better predicted from news and would leave the method contribution untouched.!!
